1.title: Writing System and User Prompts
1.text: Welcome to Module six: Writing System and User Prompts. It covers the exam area Implement A I solutions by using Microsoft Foundry. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Message roles. What goes in a system prompt. Writing an effective user prompt. The model has no memory. Safety and reliability in prompts. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Implement A I solutions by using Microsoft Foundry (fifty-five to sixty percent). Exam format: a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes; check the exam page for the time. Validated against: the official A I nine oh one study guide, current skills measured.

1.title: Message roles
1.text: Message roles. A request to a chat model is a list of messages. Each message has a role. System. Who writes it: The developer. Purpose: Sets the role, rules, tone and limits of the assistant for the whole conversation. User. Who writes it: The person using the app. Purpose: The question or task for this turn. Assistant. Who writes it: The model. Purpose: The reply; earlier replies are sent back as context.

1.title: Message roles, continued
1.text: Message roles. The system message is optional, but include at least a basic one for the best results. In some A P Is the system message is passed as instructions. Exam tip: System prompt equals standing rules from the developer ("You are a polite support assistant for Fabrikam; answer only about our products"). User prompt equals the question of the moment.

1.title: What goes in a system prompt
1.text: What goes in a system prompt. Role. "You are a travel assistant for Fabrikam Outdoors.". Scope. "Answer only questions about camping gear and our store.". Tone and style. "Be friendly and concise. Use plain English.". Format. "Reply with three bullet points." or "Return valid Jason.". Rules and safety. "If you do not know, say so. Never share personal data.". Examples. One or two sample question and answer pairs.

1.title: Writing an effective user prompt
1.text: Writing an effective user prompt. Be clear and specific. Why it helps: Less guessing. Weak versus better: "Tell me about tents" to "List three features to compare when choosing a four-person tent.". Give context. Why it helps: The model only knows what is in the prompt. Weak versus better: Add the audience, goal and data. State the format. Why it helps: Easier to use the output. Weak versus better: "Answer as a table with two columns.". Give examples (few-shot). Why it helps: Shows the pattern. Weak versus better: Add sample input and output pairs.

1.title: Writing an effective user prompt, continued
1.text: Writing an effective user prompt. Break a big task into steps. Why it helps: More reliable. Weak versus better: "First list the issues, then rank them.". Set the length. Why it helps: Avoids rambling. Weak versus better: "In under fifty words.". Provide the source text. Why it helps: Grounds the answer. Weak versus better: "Using only the text below, ". Zero-shot means no examples; one-shot and few-shot give one or several examples. Few-shot examples are sent as user and assistant messages. Few-shot tricks are not recommended for reasoning models. Exam tip: Developer rules go in the system prompt; the person's question goes in the user prompt.

1.title: The model has no memory
1.text: The model has no memory. The model does not remember earlier calls. For a conversation, the app sends the earlier messages again with each request, within the context window. Long chats cost more tokens.

1.title: Safety and reliability in prompts
1.text: Safety and reliability in prompts. Tell the model what to do when it lacks information ("If the answer is not in the text, say 'I don't know'"). This reduces made-up answers. Ground the answer in trusted text you provide. Never put secrets or personal data in a prompt unless needed and permitted. A user can try to override your rules with a prompt ("ignore the previous instructions"). This is prompt injection; keep rules in the system message and add platform safety settings. Exam tip: To make the model stay in a role and on topic to use the system prompt. To make output consistent in format to state the format and give examples. To make answers factual from your data to provide the data in the prompt.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors wants its chatbot always to answer politely and only about camping gear. Where should this rule go? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: In the system prompt. The system prompt sets the standing role, scope and tone for the conversation.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A team wants every answer returned as valid Jason with the same fields. Which approach helps most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: State the exact format and give an example in the prompt. A clear format instruction with an example makes the output consistent.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A prompt that contains two sample question and answer pairs before the real question is called what? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Few-shot. Giving several examples in the prompt is few-shot prompting.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A user asks about a policy that is not in the provided text. How should the system prompt tell the model to behave to reduce made-up answers? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Say that it does not know when the answer is not in the text. Telling the model to admit when information is missing reduces hallucinations.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which message role holds the question a customer typed? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: User. The user role holds the question or task for the current turn.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Why does a chat application send earlier messages with each new request? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: The model has no memory between calls. Each call is independent, so earlier messages must be included.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Name the three message roles. Answer: System, user and assistant. Question two. What is the system prompt for? Answer: Setting the assistant's role, rules, tone and limits. Question three. What is few-shot prompting? Answer: Giving a few examples of input and output in the prompt.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What does grounding a prompt mean? Answer: Providing trusted source text so the answer comes from it. Question five. What is prompt injection? Answer: A user prompt that tries to override the developer's rules. Question six. Why keep prompts focused? Answer: Tokens cost money and fill the context window.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Roles: system (developer rules), user (the question), assistant (the reply). System prompt: role, scope, tone, format, rules, examples. User prompt: clear, specific, context, format, steps, length, source text. Shots: zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot (examples as user and assistant messages). No memory: resend earlier messages; context window limit. Safety: say "I don't know", ground answers, no secrets in prompts, beware prompt injection. In the next module, we continue the course.
